overviewHtml:
This ungraded knowledge check assesses your understanding of the difference between software that follows written rules and software that learns from examples. You'll be asked about rule-based programs and brittleness, the parts of a machine learning system, the three kinds of learning, and generalization and overfitting.

Note: Use this to test yourself, review the feedback on any questions you miss, and retry until you feel confident before moving forward.

forms.stemHtml: A customer-service program matches each incoming message against a list of if-then rules. A customer writes in a way none of the rules cover, and the program returns an error. What does this failure show?

options.html: Overfitting, because the program fit its training examples too closely
options.text: Overfitting, because the program fit its training examples too closely
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Overfitting describes a learned model that fits the quirks of its training examples. This program has no training examples. It follows written rules, and its abrupt failure outside those rules is brittleness.

options.html: Brittleness, because it fails abruptly outside its rules
options.text: Brittleness, because it fails abruptly outside its rules
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! A rule-based system works inside the boundary of its rules and fails abruptly outside it. The uncovered message is an edge case, and the error is brittleness.

options.html: Data bias, because the program's examples were skewed
options.text: Data bias, because the program's examples were skewed
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Data bias is a slant in training data that a learned model reproduces. This program learned from no data. It follows written rules, and its abrupt failure outside those rules is brittleness.

options.html: Memorization, because the program stored past messages
options.text: Memorization, because the program stored past messages
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Memorization describes a learned model that retains its training examples individually. This program stores rules, not examples, and its abrupt failure outside those rules is brittleness.

forms.stemHtml: Which statement best describes what a trained machine learning model holds?

options.html: A complete copy of every example it was trained on
options.text: A complete copy of every example it was trained on
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. A model doesn't keep its training data and doesn't look examples up. It holds adjusted settings that summarize patterns in the data.

options.html: A list of rules its builders wrote after studying the data
options.text: A list of rules its builders wrote after studying the data
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. The builders choose the data, the design, and the goal, and they don't write the patterns. The model holds adjusted settings that summarize patterns in the data.

options.html: Adjusted settings that summarize patterns in its data
options.text: Adjusted settings that summarize patterns in its data
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Training changes the model's settings until its predictions fit the examples. The result is a compact summary of patterns, stored as numbers.

options.html: An index that points to the closest matching training example
options.text: An index that points to the closest matching training example
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. A model doesn't search its training data when it gets a new input. It holds adjusted settings that summarize patterns in the data and applies them to the input.

forms.stemHtml: A language model is trained by hiding the next word in a passage of text and having the model predict it. Which kind of learning is this?

options.html: Supervised learning, since people label each passage
options.text: Supervised learning, since people label each passage
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. No person labels the passages. The correct answer is the hidden word itself, so the data supplies its own labels. That is self-supervised learning.

options.html: Unsupervised learning, since no answers are used
options.text: Unsupervised learning, since no answers are used
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Answers are used here: the hidden word is the correct answer for each prediction. Because the data supplies its own labels, this is self-supervised learning.

options.html: Rule-based learning, since the task follows a fixed series of steps
options.text: Rule-based learning, since the task follows a fixed series of steps
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. No rules about language are written down. The model learns from examples whose correct answers come from the text itself, which is self-supervised learning.

options.html: Self-supervised learning, since the text supplies the answers
options.text: Self-supervised learning, since the text supplies the answers
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! The hidden word is the label, so no human labeling is needed. This is what lets language models learn from very large amounts of text.

forms.stemHtml: A team builds a machine learning system to find dogs in photographs. Which of these do the builders decide directly? (Select all that apply.)

options.html: Which photographs go into the training data
options.text: Which photographs go into the training data
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Choosing the data is one of the builders' decisions.

options.html: What counts as a correct prediction
options.text: What counts as a correct prediction
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! The builders set the goal that training works toward.

options.html: Which visual patterns the model uses to identify a dog
options.text: Which visual patterns the model uses to identify a dog
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. The training procedure finds the patterns. The builders learn what it found by testing the finished model.

options.html: How large the model is
options.text: How large the model is
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! The kind of model and its size are design decisions the builders make.

forms.stemHtml: A model scores very well on its training data and much worse on examples that were held back and never shown to it. What is the most likely explanation?

options.html: The model overfitted to quirks of its training examples
options.text: The model overfitted to quirks of its training examples
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! A large gap between the training score and the test score is the standard sign of overfitting. The model fit the quirks of its examples instead of the pattern they share.

options.html: The model generalized well beyond its training examples
options.text: The model generalized well beyond its training examples
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. A model that generalizes well scores well on held-back examples too. A high training score with a low test score points to overfitting.

options.html: The held-back examples were labeled by different people
options.text: The held-back examples were labeled by different people
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Nothing in the scenario says the labels differ. A high training score with a low score on held-back examples is the standard sign of overfitting.

options.html: The model was trained with unsupervised learning methods
options.text: The model was trained with unsupervised learning methods
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. The kind of learning doesn't explain a gap between two scores. A high training score with a low score on held-back examples is the standard sign of overfitting.

title: Learning from examples instead of rules
